summary: The note argues that sleep is a critical, often overlooked factor in athletic recovery and performance, citing studies on growth hormone, cortisol, cognition, and metabolism. It describes how teams use sleep trackers, sleep hygiene education, and sleep consultants, and covers challenges like travel and time zones. It closes by predicting that sleep metrics may become as important as traditional performance metrics.
one_line: Research and team practices show sleep is an active, essential driver of athletic recovery and performance, despite travel and scheduling challenges.
key_facts: A study published November 5, 2023 by the Sports Performance Research Institute examined the interplay between sleep stages and bodily repair mechanisms.
Dr. Emily Turner, a lead researcher in chronobiology and sports science, says deep sleep produces growth hormone, pivotal for tissue repair and muscle growth.
Dr. Turner's team found basketball players who increased sleep to at least nine hours improved shooting accuracy and reaction times and sustained higher performance in endurance events.
Sleep regulates the stress hormone cortisol; when exhausted, cortisol rises, inhibiting recovery and promoting muscle tissue breakdown.
A September 18, 2023 publication in the Journal of Sleep and Recovery said consistent restful sleep could help mitigate overtraining symptoms and psychological stressors.
A 2024 National Sleep Foundation study, with Dr. Martin Reed and Dr. Sarah Finch, found sleep-deprived athletes had poorer decision-making and slower cognitive processing.

Dr. Laura Krishfield of the International Institute for Sports Nutrition noted on October 14, 2023 that athletes getting 7-9 hours of quality sleep had better glucose metabolism, linked to energy efficiency and endurance.
The Phoenix Rise athletic team began integrating sleep-tracking devices in December 2023; Head Coach Jackson Peters says it lets them personalize training around individual circadian rhythms.
At the Global Sports Medicine Conference in February 2024, Dr. Nathan Richards presented research on 'sleep debt', finding strategic napping and rest can ameliorate performance drops.
Athletic departments are teaching sleep hygiene: cool, dark, quiet bedrooms and regular schedules even in the off-season.
Top-tier sports programs increasingly employ sleep consultants who work with other health professionals.

Challenges include long travel, time zone differences, competition pressure, media commitments, and early or late training sessions; proposed responses include jet lag education, adjusted travel schedules, and sleep-promoting nutrition timing.
